Intermediate and challenging problems in systems, vector spaces, transformations, projections, and eigenvectors
Matrix multiplication, elimination, rank/nullspace, bases, dot products, determinants, least squares, and eigenvectors. Mark a topic not studied when appropriate.

A parameter changes the solution set

Consider 2x + ky = 6 and 4x + 6y = 12, with real parameter k. Give the exceptional k and classify the system there. For k = 2, find x and y. At the exceptional k, change only the second right-hand side to 13 and classify again.
Eliminate a variable before dividing by a parameter expression. State what happens when that expression is zero.

Subtract twice the first equation from the second: (6 − 2k)y = 0. At k = 3 the original equations coincide. For k = 2, y = 0 and x = 3. At k = 3 with right-hand side 13, elimination gives 0 = 1, so no solution.
Try another parameter system and separate the singular matrix condition from consistency.
A complete solution, not just one vector

For the displayed A, solve Ax = (3, 6, 1)ᵀ. Let the third coordinate be the free parameter t and write x = p + td, with p₃ = 0 and d₃ = 1. Give rank, nullity, p₁, p₂, d₁, and d₂. Would replacing only the second target entry 6 by 7 leave a solution?
Show the independent equations and verify Ap = b and Ad = 0. Explain why a free variable is not an arithmetic error.

The second row is twice the first; the third row is independent. Rank 2 gives nullity 1. From y + z = 1 and x + 2y − z = 3, z = t, y = 1 − t, x = 1 + 3t. Thus p = (1,1,0), d = (3,−1,1). A target whose second entry is 7 contradicts twice its first entry.
Check a new target for compatibility before solving, then express every solution as a particular vector plus a nullspace vector.
Compose and then undo two maps
A = [[1,2],[0,1]], B = [[2,0],[1,1]], and v = (1,−1)ᵀ. Compute ABv and BAv. Which expression reverses the combined map AB?
Show each intermediate vector and explain why the reverse operation must undo the last map first.
Bv = (2,0), so ABv = (2,0). Av = (−1,−1), so BAv = (−2,−2). Both matrices are invertible; (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹ because A⁻¹ cancels the map applied last.
Use a different pair of noncommuting maps and verify the proposed inverse by multiplication.
The same map in a different basis
Let C = (u,v), where u = (1,1)ᵀ and v = (1,−1)ᵀ. In standard coordinates T(x,y) = (2x + y, 3y). For w = (4,2)ᵀ, find [w]C and [T(w)]C. Give the four entries of the matrix of T in basis C, by rows.
Keep vectors separate from their coordinate lists. Derive the columns from T(u) and T(v), then check the coordinate matrix on [w]C.

The C coordinates of (x,y) are ((x+y)/2,(x−y)/2). Thus [w]C = (3,1). T(w) = (10,6), with coordinates (8,2). T(u) = (3,3) has coordinates (3,0); T(v) = (1,−3) has coordinates (−1,2). The C matrix is [[3,−1],[0,2]].
Change a basis again and distinguish the geometric map from its matrix representation.
In Euclidean R³, project b = (2,1,3)ᵀ onto the line spanned by a = (1,2,2)ᵀ. Write the projection as ca. Give c, each residual coordinate in r = b − ca, and r·a.
Choose the coefficient by an orthogonality condition or a minimization argument. Verify the residual instead of only giving a formula.
Require (b − ca)·a = 0. Here b·a = 10 and a·a = 9, so c = 10/9. The residual is (8/9,−11/9,7/9), whose dot product with a is (8 − 22 + 14)/9 = 0.
Use a non-unit direction in a fresh projection and verify the orthogonality of the residual.
Fit a line without pretending it is exact

Use ordinary least squares with equal weights to fit y = α + βx to the three displayed points. Find α, β, and the sum of squared residuals, with residual defined as observed y minus fitted y. Can one line pass through all three points?
Construct the fit equations or centered sums. Verify that residuals sum to zero and their x-weighted sum is zero.

The normal equations are 3α + 3β = 5 and 3α + 5β = 6. Hence β = 1/2 and α = 7/6. Residuals are −1/6, 1/3, −1/6; their squares sum to 1/6. Their sum and x-weighted sum vanish. The unequal successive y changes prevent an exact line.
Compare a consistent system with an overdetermined one, and check the least-squares residual against every design column.
Eigenvectors are more than coordinate-wise ratios
For A = [[3,1],[0,2]], v = (−1,1)ᵀ, and w = (1,1)ᵀ, decide which of v and w are eigenvectors. Give the eigenvalue for v and both coordinates of A⁴v.
A common eigenvalue for all coordinates
Compute Av and Aw. For each vector, ask whether one scalar works for the whole vector, then justify the fourth power.
Av = (−2,2) = 2v. Aw = (4,2), which is not one scalar multiple of (1,1). Therefore v has eigenvalue 2 and A⁴v = 2⁴v = (−16,16). Different coordinate ratios do not define an eigenvalue.
Test another proposed eigenvector, including a zero coordinate, and justify a matrix power without four repeated multiplications.
Area change and orientation are different signs

The linear map has A = [[1,2],[3,1]]. A triangle has vertices O = (0,0), U = (2,0), and V = (0,3), listed in that order. Find det(A), the original area, and the image area. Does this ordering keep its orientation after mapping?
Use a signed determinant to reason about orientation and its magnitude to reason about area. Explain why a negative area would be the wrong interpretation.
det(A) = 1 − 6 = −5. The original area is (2×3)/2 = 3; the image area is |−5|×3 = 15. Image vertices are (0,0), (2,6), (6,3); their signed doubled area is −30, so the orientation reverses.
Map another triangle with a negative determinant and check its area using both vertex coordinates and determinant scaling.
The original triangle is dashed blue; its image is solid purple. Coordinates of the original vertices are given in the question. Both use the same coordinate scale.
An unreachable target still has a closest image
A = [[1,2],[2,4]] and b = (3,5)ᵀ. Is Ax = b consistent? Find the Euclidean closest vector p to b in the column space of A. Is an input x with Ax = p unique?
Is the input producing p unique?
Describe the column space, verify b − p is perpendicular to it, and distinguish uniqueness of the closest output from uniqueness of its input.

The column space is span((1,2)), but b has 5 ≠ 2×3. Its projection coefficient is (3 + 10)/(1 + 4) = 13/5, giving p = (13/5,26/5). The residual (2/5,−1/5) is orthogonal to (1,2). Inputs producing p are not unique because (−2,1) is a nonzero null vector.
Separate inconsistent targets, unique closest outputs, and multiple inputs to the same output.
A translation hidden inside a map
For real k, define Tₖ(x,y) = (2x + y + k, x − y). Which k makes Tₖ linear? For k = 2, u = (1,0), and v = (0,1), give the first coordinate of T₂(u + v) and of T₂(u) + T₂(v).
Give a reason that is sufficient at your chosen k and a counterexample for k = 2. Do not call every straight-line formula linear.
Tₖ(0,0) = (k,0), so k must be 0. At k = 0 the map is multiplication by [[2,1],[1,−1]], which is linear. At k = 2, T₂(u+v) = (5,0), while T₂(u)+T₂(v) = (7,0), so additivity fails.
Distinguish linear transformations from affine transformations in another formula.
A zero determinant does not finish the analysis
For Aₖ = [[1,2,1],[0,k−1,2],[0,0,k+2]], select every real k making Aₖ singular. At k = 1 give the rank, nullity, and whether A₁x = (0,0,1)ᵀ is consistent.
Compute the determinant, then inspect the actual rows at k = 1. Explain why counting nonzero diagonal entries alone can give the wrong rank.

The determinant is (k−1)(k+2), giving k = 1 or −2. At k = 1 the rows are (1,2,1), (0,0,2), (0,0,3); the last two are dependent but nonzero. Rank is 2, nullity 1. The second equation requires z = 0 and the third 3z = 1, so the target is inconsistent.
After finding an exceptional parameter, recompute rank and test the right-hand side rather than stopping at determinant zero.
For each rejected set give a specific failed condition and an example. Give independent spanning vectors for S₁ and explain the dependence in S₄.

S₁ is a homogeneous plane with basis (1,−1,0), (1,0,−1), hence dimension 2. S₂ misses zero. S₃ contains (1,0,0) and (0,1,0) but not their sum. S₄ is a line because its second spanning vector is twice the first. Thus exactly S₁ and S₄ are subspaces.
Test zero, addition, and scalar multiplication on another set before inferring a dimension.
Multi-step fraction, percentage, rate, and ratio models
Signed arithmetic, fraction operations, percentages, ratios, and a simple unknown.
Wider integer and exponent topics, and independent modelling across a full middle-school curriculum
Remove a mixture, then dilute it

Mix 3/4 litre of concentrate with 1/2 litre of water. The mixture is uniform. Remove 2/5 of the mixture, then add 1/4 litre of water. Find the concentrate fraction before removal, the litres of concentrate left after removal, and the final concentrate fraction.
A fraction of the full mixture
Track concentrate and total volume separately at every stage. Explain why removing a uniform portion alone does not change its concentration.

Initially total volume is 5/4 L and concentrate fraction is (3/4)/(5/4) = 3/5. Retaining 3/5 leaves 9/20 L concentrate and 3/4 L mixture. Adding 1/4 L water makes 1 L total, so the final fraction is 9/20.
Use a different removed fraction and distinguish a fraction of an ingredient from a fraction of the whole mixture.
Recover a price through two changing bases

A bag is discounted by 20%. An 8% sales tax is applied to its discounted price, then a $3 shipping fee is added without tax. The final charge is $46.20. Find the original price, discount amount, and tax amount.
Write a model for the final charge and reverse the operations in the correct order. State which amount is taxed.
If P is the original price, 1.08(0.8P)+3 = 46.20. Remove shipping to get 43.20, divide by 1.08 to get 40, then divide by 0.8 to get 50. The discount is 10 and tax is 0.08×40 = 3.20.
Recover an original amount after a fee and two percentage changes without adding the percentage rates.
Add filling rates, not filling times

One tap fills an empty tank in 6 hours and another in 4 hours. A leak drains a full tank in 12 hours. Assume each rate is constant and both taps and the leak operate together. Find the net tank fraction filled per hour, the time to fill an empty tank, and the fraction filled after 3/2 hours.
Use one full tank as the common unit. Explain why adding 6 and 4 does not produce a combined filling time.
The net rate is 1/6 + 1/4 − 1/12 = 1/3 tank per hour. Filling takes 1/(1/3) = 3 hours. In 3/2 hours it fills (1/3)(3/2) = 1/2 tank.
Model another process with simultaneous positive and negative rates, naming their units.
Find the counts behind a changed ratio
A club initially has boys:girls = 3:4. Six boys join and no one else joins or leaves, changing the ratio to 3:2. Find the original numbers of boys and girls and the final total membership.
Represent the original counts with one common scale. Check both the original and new ratios using the actual counts.
Write original counts as 3k and 4k. Then (3k+6)/(4k) = 3/2, giving k = 2. The counts start at 6 and 8; after joining they are 12 and 8, totaling 20.
Compare ratios by converting them to counts with a common unknown rather than adding directly to ratio terms.
Parameter systems, compound inequalities, quadratic modelling, and cost comparisons
Linear systems, absolute value, factoring quadratics, and function graphs.
A complete Algebra I syllabus, general proof, and independent modelling beyond these examples

For 2x + ky = 6 and 4x + 6y = 12, find the real k giving infinitely many solutions. For k = 2 give the unique solution. At the exceptional k, would changing 12 to 13 give one solution, no solution, or infinitely many?
Eliminate x and interpret the remaining equation before dividing. Check your unique solution in both equations.

Elimination yields (6−2k)y = 0. At k = 3 this is an identity and the lines coincide. At k = 2 it forces y = 0, giving x = 3. Changing the second right-hand side at k = 3 gives 0 = 1, hence no solution.
Distinguish an intersection, a repeated line, and parallel lines in a changed parameter system.
An absolute-value bound needs two sides
Solve |2x − 3| ≤ 5 for all real x. Give the lower and upper boundaries and decide whether both are included. A student claims x ≤ 4 alone is sufficient: does x = −2 satisfy the original inequality?
Translate the absolute-value condition into two simultaneous inequalities and test the claimed one-sided answer.
−5 ≤ 2x−3 ≤ 5 gives −2 ≤ 2x ≤ 8, hence −1 ≤ x ≤ 4. Both endpoints satisfy equality. At x = −2 the absolute value is 7, so the one-sided set includes invalid inputs.
Use a fresh absolute-value bound and verify a point outside each end.
A quadratic comes from a geometric constraint
A rectangle has perimeter 28 cm and area 45 cm². Let x be one side length. Write x² + bx + c = 0 for its possible side lengths, giving b and c, then give the longer and shorter sides.
Construct the other side from the perimeter, derive the polynomial, and check positivity, perimeter, and area.
The sides sum to 14, so x(14−x) = 45. Rearranging gives x²−14x+45 = 0 = (x−5)(x−9). The sides are 5 and 9 cm; they give perimeter 28 and area 45.
Build a new quadratic from two constraints and reject roots that do not meet the geometric conditions.
Choose a rule over a whole interval

For 0 ≤ h ≤ 8 hours, plan A costs 12 + 2h dollars and plan B costs 4 + 4h dollars. Find the break-even hours and cost. With a $25 budget and whole-number hours, find the largest affordable h under each plan.
Show the equations or inequalities. Check the next whole hour as well as the hour you select.

12+2h = 4+4h gives h = 4 and cost 20. A requires h ≤ 6.5, so the integer maximum is 6 (cost 24); 7 costs 26. B requires h ≤ 5.25, so the maximum is 5 (cost 24); 6 costs 28. Both maxima lie in the stated interval.
Compare a changed pair of fixed-fee models, including a continuous boundary and a whole-number constraint.
Plan A is the solid blue line; Plan B is the dashed purple line. Horizontal axis is hours; vertical axis is cost in dollars.

A complete geometry proof curriculum, constructions, transformations, and all circle theorems
Coordinates must support a similarity claim
A = (0,0), B = (6,0), C = (2,4). D and E are the midpoints of AB and AC. Find the area of triangle ABC, select the exact length DE, and give area(ADE)/area(ABC). Is DE parallel to BC?
Compute D and E, compare direction vectors or slopes, and explain why an area ratio is not the length ratio.

D = (3,0), E = (1,2), so DE = √(4+4) = 2√2. BC = (−4,4) is twice DE’s vector (−2,2), so the segments are parallel. ABC has area 6×4/2 = 12. The midpoint triangle has half the length scale and a quarter of the area.
Check a new coordinate midpoint construction using both a vector relation and area scaling.
Triangle ABC and its midpoint segment DE. The vertex coordinates are supplied in the question; D and E are midpoints.
A right triangle’s altitude from the right-angle vertex divides its hypotenuse into segments of 9 cm and 16 cm. Find the altitude, the shorter leg, the longer leg, and the triangle’s area.
Identify the similar triangles and justify the relationships you use. Check the legs with Pythagoras and the area by two base-height choices.
The hypotenuse is 25. Similarity gives h² = 9×16 = 144 and leg squares 25×9 = 225, 25×16 = 400. Hence h = 12 and the legs are 15,20. Area is 25×12/2 = 15×20/2 = 150.
Use a new hypotenuse split and derive, rather than merely quote, one of the similarity relationships.
Cutting a cone uses a cubic scale

A right circular cone has height 12 cm and radius 6 cm. A plane parallel to the base cuts off a smaller cone of height 4 cm measured from the original apex. Find the removed cone’s radius, its fraction of the original volume, and the remaining volume as cπ cm³ (enter c).
Coefficient c in remaining cπ cm³
Explain which cones are similar, distinguish linear and volume scales, and use the correct height for each cone.

The linear scale is 4/12 = 1/3, so the removed radius is 2 and volume fraction is (1/3)³ = 1/27. Original volume is 144π and removed volume is 16π/3, leaving 416π/3 cm³. The remaining frustum cannot be treated as a cone of height 8 and radius 6.
Compare linear, area, and volume scaling in a new parallel section before applying a volume formula.
A tangent and a secant describe one power

A circle has center O and radius 5 cm. A point P outside it satisfies OP = 13 cm. PT is tangent at T. A secant through P and O meets the near point A and far point B of the circle, in order P,A,O,B. Find PT, PA, PB, and PA×PB.
State the right angle used for the tangent and explain why the secant product uses the full PB, not just AB.

OT is perpendicular to PT, so PT² = 13²−5² = 144 and PT = 12. The ordered collinear distances give PA = 13−5 = 8 and PB = 13+5 = 18. Their product 144 equals PT²; using AB = 10 instead of PB would be incorrect.
Read a changed secant configuration and label the external and whole segments before multiplying.
Rational and logarithmic equations, multiplicities, and exponential substitutions
Factoring, domain restrictions, logarithm rules, and exponential equations.
Complex roots, full polynomial algorithms, conics, sequences, and a complete Algebra II syllabus
Solve without losing the forbidden inputs
Solve (x+1)/(x−1) = (x−1)/(x+1) + 3/2 over the real numbers. Give the smaller and larger solutions and select every input excluded by the original denominators.
State restrictions before multiplying and verify each proposed root in the original equation.
The domain excludes −1 and 1. Moving the fractions together gives 4x/(x²−1) = 3/2, hence 3x²−8x−3 = 0 = (3x+1)(x−3). Both −1/3 and 3 lie in the domain and satisfy the original equation.
Solve another rational equation and separate an algebraic root from an allowed original input.
A product equation can invent a log solution
Solve log₂(x−1) + log₂(x+3) = log₂12. Give the real solution and the other root of the polynomial obtained by combining logarithms. Is that other root a solution of the original equation?
Is the other root valid originally?
Each log argument must be positive
State both positive-argument conditions. Show the product equation and explain why a positive product alone is insufficient for two real logarithms.

The original conditions require x > 1. Combining logs gives (x−1)(x+3) = 12, or x²+2x−15 = (x−3)(x+5) = 0. Only x = 3 meets the domain; at −5 both arguments are negative even though their product is positive.
Check every original log argument after solving the combined polynomial.
For P(x) = x³ − x² − 5x − 3, select all real zeros, give the multiplicity of the zero −1, and select the full set on which P(x) > 0.
Factor and use the factor signs across every root. Explain which zero changes the sign and which does not.

P(x) = (x+1)²(x−3). Its zeros are −1 (double) and 3 (simple). The squared factor is positive except at −1; the sign is therefore the sign of x−3 elsewhere. P is positive exactly for x > 3 and does not change sign at −1.
Build a sign chart for a fresh polynomial with both odd and even root multiplicities.
An exponential substitution still has a domain
Solve 2^(2x) − 5·2^x + 4 = 0 for all real x. Give both solutions in increasing order. A student instead concludes 2^x = 5 by ignoring the constant term: is that conclusion valid?
Introduce a positive new variable, solve its polynomial, and return to x. Check both results in the original expression.
Let u = 2^x > 0. Then u²−5u+4 = (u−1)(u−4) = 0, so u = 1 or 4. These give x = 0 or 2. Setting u = 5 would leave the original expression equal to 4 rather than 0.
Solve a changed exponential polynomial and reject any substitution root outside the positive range.
Composition domains, trigonometric solution sets, rational features, and periodic models
Inequalities, composition, unit-circle values, rational functions, and trigonometric transformations.
General identities, conics, sequences, polar coordinates, and all pre-calculus topics
Both composition domains need a fresh check

Let f(t) = √(t−1) and g(x) = 1/(x−2), with real outputs. The domain of f∘g is one interval: give its lower and upper endpoints and their inclusion. For g∘f, give its lowest allowed x and its one excluded x above that boundary.
Sign analysis of a rational inequality
Write both compositions and test the signs on every interval formed by their restrictions. Do not copy either original domain without checking the outside rule.
For f(g(x)), require 1/(x−2)−1 = (3−x)/(x−2) ≥ 0 and x ≠ 2, giving 2 < x ≤ 3. For g(f(x)), require x ≥ 1 and √(x−1) ≠ 2, hence exclude x = 5. The boundary x = 1 is allowed.
Compare the domains of two new composition orders by tracking the input of the outside function.
Return from a quadratic to every angle
Solve 2 sin²θ − sinθ − 1 = 0 on 0 ≤ θ < 2π. Select all solutions; angle labels are coefficients of π.
All quadrants after a trigonometric substitution
Factor in sinθ, then use the stated interval to list every angle for each admissible sine value.
(2sinθ+1)(sinθ−1) = 0 gives sinθ = −1/2 or 1. On this interval, −1/2 gives 7π/6 and 11π/6, while 1 gives π/2. Exactly those three angles solve the original equation.
Solve a changed trigonometric polynomial and distinguish algebraic sine values from all corresponding angles.
A cancelled factor leaves a hole
For R(x) = (x²−1)/(x²−3x+2), give the x and y coordinates of its removable hole, its vertical asymptote x-value, horizontal asymptote y-value, and x-intercept.
Factor both polynomials, retain original exclusions, and explain why the two excluded inputs have different graph features.

R simplifies to (x+1)/(x−2) only for x ≠ 1,2. At x = 1 the limiting y is −2, giving hole (1,−2). At x = 2 the denominator still vanishes while the numerator does not, giving a vertical asymptote. Equal original degrees give horizontal asymptote y = 1, and x = −1 is the allowed zero.
Classify every original exclusion as a hole or asymptote and verify the resulting intercepts.
Interpret a periodic model across a full cycle
A height model is h(t) = 5 + 3 cos(πt/6), with t in hours and 0 ≤ t ≤ 12. Give its period, first time h(t) = 5, minimum height, and earliest time the minimum occurs.
Identify the midline and amplitude, then solve the angle conditions in the given interval. Explain why the coefficient of t is not the period.
A full cosine cycle requires (π/6)T = 2π, so T = 12. The first zero of cosine occurs at angle π/2, giving t = 3. The minimum is 5−3 = 2 and first occurs at angle π, giving t = 6.
Analyze a shifted periodic model and check the first solution against its phase and interval.
Differentiability constraints, optimization, signed motion, and accumulation from a graph
Limits, continuity, differentiation rules, definite integrals, extrema, and the fundamental theorem of calculus.
General integration methods, multivariable calculus, differential equations, and rigorous limit proofs
Continuity is only the first condition
Define f(x) = ax² + b for x < 1 and f(x) = 3x − 1 for x ≥ 1. Find a and b so f is differentiable at x = 1, then give f′(1).
Write the separate continuity and slope conditions. Explain why satisfying only the value condition cannot establish differentiability.
Continuity requires a+b = 2. Equality of one-sided slopes requires 2a = 3, so a = 3/2 and b = 1/2. The common derivative is 3. These conditions also make the difference quotients agree at the join.
Choose constants for a fresh piecewise function by checking both value limits and derivative limits.
Find a global maximum with endpoints
On 0 ≤ x ≤ 4, let f(x) = x²e^(−x). Give the x-location of its global maximum and m such that the maximum value is m e^(−2). Give c such that f′(3) = c e^(−3).
Differentiate, find the interior critical points, compare endpoints, and justify the maximum by a sign or value argument.

f′(x) = e^(−x)x(2−x). It is positive on (0,2) and negative on (2,4), so the global maximum is at 2 with value 4e^(−2), above both endpoints. At 3 the derivative is −3e^(−3). The endpoint 0 has value 0; a zero derivative alone does not identify a maximum.
Analyze a changed exponential product on a closed interval and include all endpoints in the reasoning.
Distance needs the internal sign changes
A particle has velocity v(t) = t² − 4t + 3 metres per second for 0 ≤ t ≤ 4 seconds and starts at position 5 metres. Give its net displacement, total distance travelled, and final position.
Find every change of velocity sign before integrating. State why final position and total distance are different quantities.

v = (t−1)(t−3), positive on (0,1) and (3,4), negative on (1,3). The antiderivative is t³/3−2t²+3t. The three signed contributions are 4/3, −4/3, 4/3. Net displacement is 4/3, distance is 4, and final position is 5+4/3 = 19/3.
Split a fresh motion integral at every velocity zero and compare signed displacement with distance.
The accumulation maximum is not the tallest point

On [0,6], f is the continuous piecewise-linear graph joining (0,2), (2,−2), (4,0), (6,2). Let F(x) = ∫₀ˣ f(t) dt. Give the global maximum location and value of F, its global minimum location and value, and F′(3).
Sign of the integrand and accumulation extrema
Use the sign of f for increasing/decreasing F, calculate the necessary signed regions, and compare the endpoints. Distinguish f(3) from F(3).

f crosses zero at 1 and 4. F increases to x = 1, decreases until 4, then increases. F(1) = 1, F(2) = 0, F(4) = −2, F(6) = 0, and F(0) = 0. Thus the global maximum is (1,1), minimum (4,−2). The theorem gives F′(3) = f(3) = −1.
Analyze a new sign-changing integrand and predict its accumulation graph before calculating areas.
Graph of f, not F: straight segments join the four stated points. Horizontal axis is t; vertical axis is f(t).
Reverse conditional probability, aggregation, sample spread, and regression diagnostics
Conditional probability, two-way tables, sample variance, transformations, and least-squares regression.
Sampling distributions, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, time series, and all study-design assumptions

A batch contains exactly 1,000 components, of which 100 are faulty. A screening rule flags 90% of the faulty components and 5% of the other 900. Select one flagged component uniformly. Find the number of false flags, total flags, and probability it is faulty.
Construct counts for both groups and identify the denominator for selection among flags. Explain why the answer is not 90%.

There are 90 faulty flags and 0.05×900 = 45 nonfaulty flags. Of the 135 total flags, 90 are faulty, so the conditional probability is 90/135 = 2/3. The 90% rate conditions on faulty items, not on flags.
Use changed base rates and keep P(flagged | faulty) separate from P(faulty | flagged).
Group comparisons can reverse when combined

The table gives successes and total attempts for methods A and B in two difficulty groups. Find each method’s overall success rate. Does A have the higher success rate within both groups? Does the table alone prove A causes a better outcome?
Does the table alone prove causation?
Calculate both within-group comparisons and show the overall numerators and denominators. Explain the different group allocations and the missing design information.

Within the first group A has 18/20 = 0.90 versus B’s 80/100 = 0.80; within the second A has 10/100 = 0.10 versus 1/20 = 0.05. Overall A has 28/120 = 7/30 while B has 81/120 = 27/40. Their allocation to difficulty groups differs, reversing the aggregate comparison. No random assignment or confounding control is stated.
Compare new stratified and pooled rates before recommending a method or making a causal claim.
The sample is 1, 2, 4, 5. Compute its mean and sample variance (using n−1). Transform every observation by Y = 2X−1. Give the new mean and new sample variance.
Construct the deviations rather than using a supplied sum. Explain separately the effect of the shift and the factor 2.

Mean is 3, with deviations −2,−1,1,2 and squared sum 10. Sample variance is 10/3. The transformed data are 1,3,7,9, with mean 5 and deviations −4,−2,2,4, squared sum 40. Variance is 40/3; shifting changes the center, while scaling by 2 multiplies variance by 4.
Apply another affine transformation and check variance directly as well as through the scaling rule.
Fit, inspect a residual, and interpret r²
Fit ordinary equal-weight least-squares regression y = a + bx to (1,2), (2,1), (3,4). Give b, a, the residual at x = 2 (observed minus fitted), and r².

Compute the centered sums, verify residuals sum to zero, and explain what r² describes without treating it as a causal effect or the fraction of correct predictions.

Initial potential energy relative to final level (J)

Accounting for the stated thermal energy

Three of four equal parts and six of eight equal parts cover the same fraction of an unchanged whole. Both numerator and denominator multiply by 2.
For the same whole, 1/2 + 1/4 = 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4. The denominator names the part size; it is not added.
Explain why 2/6 is not the sum of 1/2 and 1/4.
Multiplication can describe part of a part.
Half of three quarters is 3/8 of the original whole. Splitting each quarter in half produces eighths.
Which fraction equals 3/4 for the same whole?
Multiply numerator and denominator by 2; the share stays unchanged.
For the same whole, what is 1/3 + 1/6?
What fraction of a whole is half of 2/3?
Draw one fixed whole and show equivalent fractions, a sum, and a part of a part.
What stays constant in a proportional relationship?
Connect a ratio, a unit rate, and a multiplicative rule.
Keep the two quantities and units.
A unit rate tells how much of one quantity corresponds to one unit of another. Here it is dollars per item.
Read the cost for exactly one item.
At $3 per item, two items cost $6 and five items cost $15. The cost-to-item ratio is unchanged.
25% of 80 means 25/100 × 80 = 20. The percentage names a relative share, while 20 is an amount.
Find 10% of 80, then compare it with 25%.
Watch for a fixed starting fee.
A $2 delivery fee plus $3 per item gives cost = 2 + 3n. The total cost per item then changes with n, so total cost is not proportional to item count.
Compare one-item and two-item total cost when a fixed fee is added.
Three notebooks cost $12 with no fixed fee. What is the unit price?
Which total cost rule is proportional to the number of items n?
C/n = 5 stays constant for positive n, and the rule has no fixed fee.
Compare a unit-price rule with a rule that includes a fixed fee.
How is an expression different from an equation?
Substitute values, combine like terms, and keep operations in order.
2x + 3 is an expression. Choosing x supplies an input; it does not ask you to solve an equation.
Try a negative input and keep its sign.
Combine terms with the same variable part.
3x + 2x = 5x, but 3x + 2 cannot be combined as 5x. The constant does not count another x.
2(x + 3) = 2x + 6 because both terms inside the parentheses are multiplied by 2.
Use x = 1 to check both forms.
Which expression equals 4a + 3a − 2 for every a?
The two variable terms combine to 7a; the constant remains −2.
Which expression equals 3(y − 2) for every y?
Evaluate two equivalent expressions at a positive and a negative input.
Solve a linear equation and verify the solution in the original.
An equation says two expressions have equal values. A solution is an input that makes this statement true.
Read both sides of the displayed equation.
For 2x + 3 = 11, subtract 3 from both sides to get 2x = 8. Changing only one side would not preserve equality.
Name the operation applied to both sides.
Divide both sides of 2x = 8 by 2 to obtain x = 4. Reversible operations preserve the solution set here.
Choose another example solution and follow both steps.
At x = 4, 2(4) + 3 = 11. Checking the original helps detect arithmetic or sign errors.
Check your chosen solution before moving on.
Subtract 3, then divide by 2; substitution gives 11.
Add 5 to both sides: 3x = 15; divide by 3.
Divide by 4 to get x − 2 = 3, then add 2.
Solve a changed equation by two valid routes and check both results.
What do slope and intercept tell you?
Connect a rule, a graph, and a constant rate of change.
Read a rule as input and output.
In y = mx + b, each x determines one y. Plotting the pairs makes the relationship visible.
The intercept is the output at zero.
At x = 0, mx vanishes and y = b. The point (0, b) is the y-intercept.
Change b while keeping m fixed.
Slope is change in y divided by change in x. A slope of 2 means y increases by 2 for every increase of 1 in x.
Change m and compare the direction of the line.
Zero slope is still a function.
When m = 0, y = b is horizontal. Every input has the same output; the graph is not a vertical line.
Set m = 0, then compare with m = −1.
For y = 3x − 2, what is the y-intercept?
A line passes through (1, 2) and (4, 8). What is its slope?
Which rule has output decreasing by 4 when input increases by 1?
The coefficient −4 is the constant output change per input unit.
Build a line from an intercept and rate, then verify a second point.
What does a shared solution mean?
Find and check a pair that satisfies two equations at once.
A system asks for a pair (x, y) that satisfies both equations. A solution to only one equation is not enough.
Read y = x + 2 and the second rule.
At a crossing, the same x gives the same y in both rules. For y = x + 2 and y = −x + 6, x = 2 and y = 4.
Check both rules at the intersection.
Set x + 2 = −x + 6, collect 2x = 4, then get x = 2. Substitute to obtain y = 4.
Change the second intercept and find the new pair.
Distinct parallel lines have no common solution. Identical lines have infinitely many common points. A graph window alone may hide an intersection.
Compare y = x + 2 with y = x + 5 on paper.
For y = x + 1 and y = −x + 5, which pair satisfies both?
Solve x + y = 9 and x − y = 3.
Adding yields 2x = 12; then y = 3. Both original equations hold.
How many solutions do y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x − 4 have?
The slopes match but intercepts differ; equating outputs would give 1 = −4.
Check a proposed pair in each original equation, including a no-solution example.
Why does a factor reveal a zero?
Use the zero-product rule and distinguish zeros from the vertex.
A zero is an input with output zero.
A graph zero lies on the x-axis. It is an x-value, not necessarily a turning point.
A zero product has a zero factor.
For (x − 1)(x − 4) = 0, at least one factor must be zero: x = 1 or x = 4.
Change the second root and inspect the factors.
x² − 9 = (x − 3)(x + 3), so both 3 and −3 are roots. Taking only the positive square root loses one solution.
Check the original and distinguish the vertex.
For two distinct roots, the vertex lies midway between their x-values for a quadratic. Its output generally differs from zero.
Compare a crossing with the lowest point of this parabola.
Either factor can be zero; both roots belong in the solution set.
Solve x² = 16 over the real numbers.
For y = (x + 1)(x − 3), which statement describes the zeros?
The graph crosses the x-axis at x = −1 and x = 3.
Set each factor to zero. The y-intercept is −3, and the vertex is a different point.
Factor a new quadratic, list every root, and verify by substitution.
Which relationships determine an unknown angle?
Use straight-line and vertical-angle relationships with reasons.
Identify the shared vertex and rays.
An angle describes the turn between two rays with a shared endpoint. Angle measure is independent of how long the drawn rays are.
Identify the vertex before reading the measure.
Two adjacent angles whose outer rays form a straight line add to 180°. An arbitrary adjacent pair need not do so.
Change one angle and find the other.
When two straight lines cross, opposite angles are equal. Each is supplementary to the same adjacent angle.
Draw crossed lines and explain why the opposite measures match.
A reason such as “they look equal” is weaker than identifying vertical angles or a straight line. Drawings may not be to scale.
Explain which relationship would still hold if the drawing changed.
Two adjacent angles form a straight line. One is 65°. What is the other?
Two straight lines cross. An angle is 38°. What is its vertically opposite angle?
Vertical angles are equal; 142° is the adjacent supplement.
Two angles are adjacent, with no other information. Must they sum to 180°?
No; their outer rays must form a straight line.
Yes; all adjacent angles are supplementary.
No; adjacent angles always sum to 90°.
Adjacency alone does not specify a straight turn.
For an unknown angle, name the relationship and its geometric conditions.
When does the Pythagorean relationship apply?
Identify a right triangle, its legs, and its hypotenuse.
The equation a² + b² = c² applies to a right triangle, where c is opposite the 90° angle.
With legs 3 and 4, c² = 9 + 16 = 25, so c = 5 because a length is positive.
Change a leg and compare c with both legs.
A hypotenuse is not another leg.
When a hypotenuse and one leg are known, subtract the known leg square from c². Adding them would find the wrong quantity.
For c = 13 and one leg = 5, compute the other leg.
The interior angles of a Euclidean triangle sum to 180°. A right triangle therefore has two acute angles summing to 90°, but their individual values need not be equal.
Give two different acute-angle pairs for right triangles.
A right triangle has legs 6 and 8. What is its hypotenuse?
A right triangle has hypotenuse 13 and one leg 5. What is the other leg?
The unknown leg square is 169 − 25 = 144, so its length is 12.
A triangle has angles 47° and 68°. What is the third interior angle?
Identify the known and unknown triangle quantities before choosing a relationship.
How do lengths and areas scale?
Use corresponding lengths and separate scale factors for length and area.
Similar figures have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding lengths. Correspondence determines which ratios can be compared.
Read original width and scaled width in the table.
A length scale factor of 2 changes a 3-by-2 rectangle to 6-by-4. Its perimeter also doubles.
Both width and height multiply by k, so their product multiplies by k². Doubling lengths quadruples area.
Similar figures can differ in size. Congruent figures have matching shape and size; their corresponding lengths agree.
Explain what is special about k = 1.
Similar triangles have corresponding sides 4 and 10. What is the scale factor from the first to the second?
Every length of a figure is multiplied by 3. What happens to its area?
Area has two length dimensions, each scaled by 3.
Must two similar triangles be congruent?
Yes; equal angles force equal lengths.
No; similar triangles never have equal angles.
Similarity fixes shape and length ratios; congruence also fixes size.
Match corresponding sides, then predict length, perimeter, and area changes.
Which quantity does the calculation measure?
Separate area, perimeter, and volume and attach the correct units.
A rectangle with width w and height h has perimeter 2w + 2h, measured in length units.
Trace all four sides of the rectangle.
The rectangle area is wh, measured in square units. The same area can accompany different perimeters.
Compare widths 4 and 6 with a fixed height.
A triangle uses half a base-height rectangle.
Triangle area is bh/2 when h is perpendicular to the chosen base. A slanted side is not automatically the height.
Draw a perpendicular height for a new triangle.
Volume introduces a third length dimension.
A rectangular prism has volume lwh in cubic units. Keeping units visible helps distinguish a boundary, surface, and solid amount.
Find the volume of a 2-by-3-by-4 prism.
A rectangle measures 7 cm by 3 cm. What is its perimeter?
A triangle has base 8 m and perpendicular height 5 m. What is its area?
A rectangular prism measures 2 cm by 3 cm by 5 cm. What is its volume?
For a new figure, identify whether the question asks for boundary, surface, or volume.
What does a polynomial factor tell you?
Connect factors, roots, and the number of distinct zeros.
A factor describes a multiplicative piece.
The product (x + 1)(x − 1)(x − 3) is a cubic polynomial because its highest-power term is x³.
Locate each factor and its zero.
The zeros are −1, 1, and 3. Changing one factor changes its corresponding root.
Change the third root while holding the others fixed.
Repeated factors do not create new distinct roots.
(x − 2)²(x + 1) has degree 3 but only two distinct real roots: 2 and −1. Multiplicity counts repeats.
List both distinct roots and their multiplicities.
Not all roots must be real.
x² + 1 has no real zero because x² is nonnegative for real x. It has complex roots, which this first lesson does not develop.
Explain why a graph with no real crossing need not be a constant function.
What are the distinct real zeros of (x + 2)(x − 1)(x − 4)?
Set each factor to zero and keep all three roots.
How many distinct real zeros does (x − 3)²(x + 1) have?
The root 3 repeats, but distinct roots are 3 and −1.
Which polynomial has no real zero?
For real x, x² + 4 ≥ 4, so it cannot equal zero.
Compare a polynomial’s degree, distinct roots, and repeated factors.
Keep original domain restrictions when simplifying rational expressions.
In (x² − 4)/(x − 2), the original expression is undefined at x = 2.
Check the denominator at the middle table input.
x² − 4 = (x − 2)(x + 2). For x ≠ 2, canceling the nonzero common factor leaves x + 2.
Read the simplified rule together with the restriction.
An equivalent rule needs its domain.
The unrestricted line y = x + 2 includes (2, 4); the original rational function does not. The simplified formula does not fill the hole.
Compare evaluating the original with evaluating the unrestricted line.
Cancel factors rather than individual terms.
In (x + 2)/x, the x is not a common factor of the entire numerator. For nonzero x the rule is 1 + 2/x, not 2.
Factor the numerator; cancel only for x ≠ 3, preserving that exclusion.
At x = 4, what is the value of (x² − 16)/(x − 4)?
The original denominator is zero at 4, even though x + 4 is the simplified rule elsewhere.
Divide both numerator terms by x; there is no common x factor to cancel from x + 5.
State original exclusions before simplifying, then check one excluded and one allowed input.
Distinguish a repeated factor from a repeated fixed difference.
In y = 100bᵗ, the initial amount at t = 0 is 100 because b⁰ = 1.
A 20% increase keeps the original 100% and adds 20%, giving factor 1.20. A 20% decrease gives factor 0.80.
Compare the growth and decay settings.
Repeat the factor for each period.
After two 20% increases, 100 × 1.2² = 144. Adding a fixed 20 twice gives 140 and describes a different model.
Read the amounts at t = 1 and t = 2.
A constant percentage model assumes the same proportional change each period. Real quantities may not follow it indefinitely.
Give a situation in which the rate might change.
An amount of 80 grows by 25% each period. What is it after two periods?
An amount of 200 loses 10% of its current value each hour. What remains after two hours?
Which rule represents an initial amount of 50 growing by 8% per period t?
1.08 is the multiplicative factor that retains 100% and adds 8%.
Write the starting amount and factor before predicting a later amount.
Interpret a logarithm as an inverse question and preserve its domain.
2³ = 8 asks for the output of a known exponent. log₂8 = 3 asks for the exponent that gives 8.
Read the power table in both directions.
log₃27 = 3 because 3³ = 27. Changing the base changes the inverse question.
Compare the same exponent in the different base settings.
For real logarithms with base b > 0 and b ≠ 1, the argument must be positive. In log₂(x − 1), this requires x > 1.
A product rule does not become a sum rule.
For positive u and v, log_b(uv) = log_b(u) + log_b(v). There is no corresponding rule replacing log_b(u + v) by this sum.
Compare log₂(2 + 2) with log₂2 + log₂2, then try 2 + 6.
What is the real domain of log₂(x − 5)?
The argument must be strictly positive: x − 5 > 0.
Which identity holds for every positive u and v?
The product rule follows by adding exponents. The quotient rule subtracts logarithms.
Translate a logarithm to a power equation and check the argument restrictions.

Selected data summaries, study design, standardization, and elementary probability
A survey records shirt color and commute time in minutes. Which variable has numerical differences with a meaningful size?
Explain why coding colors with numbers would not make their differences measured amounts.
Commute time is quantitative. Color is categorical; assigning number labels to colors does not create a measured numerical distance.
Distinguish a measurement from a category label.
A table gives waiting times and counts. How many cases were measured, and how many waited at most 2 minutes?
Explain what is added to find the number of cases.
Add counts: 2 + 3 + 1 = 6 total. The first two counts sum to 5 cases at most 2 minutes.
Keep measured values separate from their frequencies.
Sales are 98 units in A and 100 in B. A bar chart starts its vertical axis at 97, making the visible bars 1 and 3 units tall. Which claim describes the actual sales?
B sold 2 more units, about 2.04% more than A.
B sold three times as many units as A.
A and B sold the same amount.
Explain how a truncated baseline changes visible lengths without changing the values.
The sales difference is 100 − 98 = 2; 2/98 is about 2.04%. A truncated bar baseline exaggerates the visual ratio.
Read the scale and baseline before comparing bar lengths.
The observations are 2, 3, 3, 4, 18. Find their mean and median.
Show the total and the middle sorted position; explain why the summaries differ.
The total is 30 across five observations, giving mean 6. The third sorted value is 3. The large value raises the mean.
Calculate and interpret two centers before choosing one.
The sorted values are 1, 3, 7, 9. Find the median.
Explain why neither middle observation alone is the median here.
For four values, average the second and third: (3 + 7)/2 = 5.
Use both central positions for an even number of observations.
Two students average 80 points and eight other students average 90. What is the mean across all ten students?
Use each group size to reconstruct the total; explain why averaging 80 and 90 equally fails.
The total is 2 × 80 + 8 × 90 = 880. Divide by 10 to obtain 88. The groups have unequal weights.
Weight each group mean by its number of cases.
Data A: 4, 5, 6. Data B: 1, 5, 9. Find each range.
Compare their common mean with their different spreads.
Both means are 5. Range A is 6 − 4 = 2; range B is 9 − 1 = 8. The common center does not imply equal spread.
Compare variation as well as center.
The sample is 1, 3, 5, with mean 3. The sum of squared deviations is 8. Sample variance uses divisor n − 1. Find the sample variance and standard deviation.
Explain the divisor and the square root; identify the units of each quantity.
n = 3, so sample variance is 8/2 = 4. Sample standard deviation is √4 = 2 in the original measurement units; variance has squared units.
Keep variance separate from its square root.
A score is 20, the reference mean is 14, and the standard deviation is 3. Find z = (score − mean)/standard deviation.
Explain the sign and what the number counts.
z = (20 − 14)/3 = 2, meaning two standard deviations above the reference mean.
Translate a standardized distance into an interpretation.
An online poll asks visitors to a cycling club website whether city residents want bike lanes. What is a likely problem?
Visitors and volunteers may differ from city residents overall.
Only having fewer than one million responses could cause bias.
All online responses are random samples.
Name the target population and the people actually reached.
The target is city residents, but the poll reaches volunteering website visitors interested in cycling. A large response count does not repair this selection mismatch.
Separate the population from the sampling frame and response process.
A random sample of students reports existing exercise hours and grades. Was a treatment randomly assigned?
Explain which part was randomized and why it does not remove all confounding.
Students were randomly selected; their exercise was observed, not assigned. Other factors can explain an exercise-grade association.
Identify each random step before making a causal claim.
Volunteers are randomly assigned to tutoring A or B in a well-run trial. Choose the careful conclusion.
A causal comparison for participants may be supported; wider generalization needs care.
All students are represented because assignment was random.
Explain how recruitment and assignment affect different claims.
Random assignment supports the treatment comparison, while volunteer recruitment may limit population generalization.
Evaluate causation and population coverage separately.
Keep the whole or condition on a group
A student is selected uniformly from the table. Find P(club and pass) and P(pass given club). Fractions are accepted.
Explain why the numerators match but the denominators differ.
There are 8 in the overlap among 50 students: 8/50 = 0.16. There are 20 club members: 8/20 = 0.4.
Name the reference group before dividing.
Use the same table and uniform selection. Find P(club given pass). Is it equal to P(pass given club)?
Identify all students who passed before counting the club members among them.
There are 18 who passed and 8 of them are club members, so the probability is 8/18 = 4/9. It differs from 8/20 = 0.4.
Do not reverse a conditional probability without changing the denominator.
Count a union without double counting
P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.3, and P(A and B) = 0.1. Find P(A or B), where “or” includes the overlap. Are A and B independent?
Explain both the overlap subtraction and your independence comparison.
The union is 0.4 + 0.3 − 0.1 = 0.6. Independence would require 0.4 × 0.3 = 0.12 for the overlap; the given 0.1 differs.
Separate a union rule from an independence condition.
Selected algebra, function domains, composition, graph features, trigonometry, and exponential/logarithmic rules
For every real x, which expression equals x² × x³?
Explain using repeated multiplication or the exponent rule.
The factors contain five copies of x in total, so the product is x⁵.
Distinguish multiplying powers from taking a power of a power.
Keep an excluded input after cancellation
For f(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2), give the simplified rule on its original domain and the excluded input.
x + 2 for every real x, including 2
Explain why simplifying does not supply a value at the zero denominator.
Factor the numerator as (x − 2)(x + 2), then cancel for x ≠ 2. The original denominator is still zero at 2.
Explain what division by a negative number does to the comparison, and check a value.
Dividing both sides by −2 reverses the sign: x > −3. For example x = 0 satisfies the original inequality.
Keep the direction and strict boundary correct.
For real-valued f(x) = √(x − 3), select the domain.
Use the radicand condition and check x = 3.
x − 3 must be nonnegative; at x = 3 the value is 0. Thus x ≥ 3.
Distinguish an included radical boundary from an excluded denominator.
Let f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x². Find f(g(2)) and g(f(2)).
Show each intermediate output before applying the outside function.
g(2) = 4 and f(4) = 9. f(2) = 5 and g(5) = 25. Composition order matters.
Name the inside and outside rules before calculating.
The rule is y = 3x − 2. Choose its inverse rule, and recover x when y = 13.
Explain the reverse operations and check the original rule.
Add 2 to y, then divide by 3. For y = 13, x = 15/3 = 5; 3 × 5 − 2 = 13.
Reverse the operations in reverse order.
For y = −2(x + 1)² + 3, give the vertex coordinates and opening direction.
Explain which terms give the vertex and which gives the direction.
Write x + 1 as x − (−1). The vertex is (−1, 3), and the negative outside multiplier makes it open downward.
Connect each parameter with a graph feature.
Select every zero of f(x) = x² − 5x + 6.
Factor the expression and check each zero by substitution.
x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3). Exactly x = 2 and x = 3 make the product zero.
Find every factor’s zero without treating an intercept as a vertex.
For f(x) = x² over the interval [1, 3], find [f(3) − f(1)]/(3 − 1).
Show the output difference and input difference; distinguish this from the output f(3).
The output change is 9 − 1 = 8 across input change 2, so the average rate is 4. This is a secant slope.
Separate output height from change per input unit.
Write 150° as cπ radians. Enter c, using a fraction if useful.
Convert angle units before using radian formulas.
At 120°, the unit-circle point lies in quadrant II. Select the signs of cosine and sine.
Connect cosine to horizontal position and sine to vertical position.
Quadrant II has x < 0 and y > 0. Cosine is the x-coordinate and sine is the y-coordinate.
Use coordinate signs instead of memorizing isolated signs.
An angle in quadrant I has cos θ = 3/5. Find sin θ.
Use sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 and justify the chosen sign.
sin²θ = 1 − 9/25 = 16/25. Quadrant I makes sine positive, giving 4/5.
Use the identity and quadrant information together.
Turn percent growth into a factor
An amount begins at 80 and grows by 25% per period. Give the growth factor and the amount after two periods.
Explain why the percentage multiplies the current amount each time.
The factor is 1 + 0.25 = 1.25. Two periods give 80 × 1.25² = 125.
Keep the factor separate from the percent and the amount added.
An amount begins at 200 and loses 10% of its current value each hour. Find the amount after two hours.
Show the factor and both successive amounts; explain why subtracting a fixed 20 twice differs.
Use a repeated ratio for percentage decay.
Interpret a logarithm and its domain
Find log₂32. For real log₂(x − 1), choose the domain.
Explain the exponent question and why the logarithm argument must be positive.
2⁵ = 32, so log₂32 = 5. The argument x − 1 must be positive, giving x > 1.
Connect logarithms to exponents and preserve their positive-input restriction.

Read position, signed velocity, and acceleration as different quantities.
Choose a reference and a direction.
Position tells where an object is relative to a chosen origin. Here the positive direction is east and time is in seconds. The height of a position graph is not the height of the ground.
Keep velocity at +2 m/s. If the starting position changes from 0 m to 4 m, will the runner travel farther in 4 s?
Compare those two settings. Check the line, the final position, and the distance readout.
What changes, and what stays the same? Use the graph to support your prediction or revise it.
For constant velocity, x = x₀ + vt. Velocity is the signed change in position divided by elapsed time. Its sign describes direction; position describes location.
Start at 8 m with velocity −2 m/s. Predict the positions at 1 s and 3 s. Can a runner be east of the origin while moving west?
Set those controls and use two points on the line to check your predicted positions.
Explain the difference between a positive position and a positive velocity. An equation or two marked points can be enough.

Displacement is final position minus initial position. Distance counts the whole route and cannot be negative. For one constant-velocity segment, distance = |v|t. A trip that turns around needs the distances of all segments.
Starting at 4 m, compare velocities +2 m/s and −2 m/s over 4 s. Predict which quantities will agree and which will differ.
Check both settings. Then sketch a separate trip: 4 m east followed by 4 m west. The straight-line control cannot draw that turnaround.
Compare distance and displacement for all three trips. What goes wrong with the claim that zero displacement means no travel?
For the return trip, add both segment lengths for distance; compare the final and initial positions for displacement.
Check what an end point can tell you.
A straight position–time line means constant velocity and zero acceleration in this model. Average acceleration is Δv/Δt. A final position alone does not tell you the earlier motion.
Can two different constant-velocity trips both finish at x = 8 m after 4 s?
Find two settings with different starting positions and velocities that do this. Check their graphs and readouts.
Show why they share an end point but not the same motion. What extra time-stamped position would distinguish them? Why is acceleration zero in both model trips?
Use 8 = x₀ + 4v. Pick a starting position first, then solve for a velocity within the control range.
A runner is 4 m east of an origin at t = 0 and 10 m east at t = 3 s. What is the average velocity?
(10−4)/3 = +2 m/s. Subtract the starting position before dividing by time.
A runner moves from x = 8 m to x = 2 m in 3 s at constant velocity. Which pair is correct?
Velocity = (2−8)/3 = −2 m/s. It stays constant, so acceleration is zero.
A runner travels 12 m east, then 5 m west. What are distance and displacement?
Distance adds lengths: 12+5=17 m. Signed displacement is 12−5=+7 m.
Use a new position table. State the direction and units before calculating a rate.
Use the net force and compare fair tests of Fnet = ma.
Add forces on the same object.
Choose east as positive. Add the signed horizontal forces on this cart to find Fnet. Fnet = ma uses this total, not just the largest force. Vertical forces balance in this model.
Keep mass at 2 kg and the eastward force at 6 N. Predict the net force when the westward force is 2 N, then 6 N.
Compare both settings and the acceleration readout.
Why can the cart have two nonzero forces on it but zero acceleration?
Use a = Fnet/m. The sign describes acceleration, not necessarily the current direction of motion. To investigate mass, keep both horizontal forces fixed.
Keep the eastward force at 6 N and westward force at 2 N. Predict how acceleration changes when mass goes from 2 kg to 4 kg.
Check those settings, then calculate acceleration independently from net force and mass.
Which variable did you change, and which did you hold fixed? Would this comparison tell you the cart’s current velocity?
Balanced forces do not require rest.
Zero net force means zero acceleration. To predict velocity, you also need an initial velocity. For a constant acceleration, v = v₀ + at; a force diagram alone supplies no v₀.
With balanced forces, could one cart stay at rest while another keeps moving east?
Set both forces to 4 N and mass to 2 kg. On paper, use v₀ = 0 m/s for one cart and +3 m/s for the other; predict each velocity after 2 s.

The median is the middle sorted observation, or the average of the two middle observations for an even count. In 1, 2, 2, 3, 12, the median is 2. A larger maximum can pull the mean upward while the middle value stays unchanged.
Explain why moving only the largest of these nine observations leaves the median at 4.
A center does not show all variation.

The range is maximum minus minimum. Two data sets can share a mean or median but have different spreads. Standard deviation measures spread around the mean; its sample and population formulas use different divisors. We do not calculate it in these lessons.
Compare the smallest and largest observations, then calculate the range.
Choose a summary for the question.

A resistant center such as the median can describe a typical case when there is a long tail. The mean remains useful for totals and averages across all cases. Neither choice permits removing an inconvenient observation without investigating it.
Describe a situation where the mean and median answer different questions.
For these five values, which pair is correct?
The total is 20, so the mean is 4. The middle sorted value is 2.
There are four values, so average the two middle values: (4 + 4)/2 = 4.
Replace 9 with 29 in this data set. What happens?
The mean and range increase; the median stays 4.
Only one of five values increases by 20, so the mean increases by 4. The range increases by 20. The middle value stays 4.
Find two data sets with the same center but different spreads, and justify which summaries to report.
Who was included, and what was assigned?
Separate random selection, random assignment, and unsupported causal claims.

A sample is the group measured; a population is the group we want to describe. A dorm-based volunteer survey may miss commuters and people who decline. A larger sample does not by itself repair an incomplete sampling frame or nonresponse bias.
Compare the campus population with the illustrative selected group. Who may be missing?

Random selection from an adequate population list gives cases a known chance of inclusion. It supports population estimation, with sampling uncertainty and possible nonresponse still considered. One balanced-looking sample is not proof of random selection; a random sample need not be exactly balanced.
Switch selection methods. Read the method, not just the two bar heights.

Random assignment determines who receives which treatment. In a well-run experiment it helps balance confounding factors and supports a causal comparison. It does not make volunteers representative of all students. Random selection and random assignment do different jobs.
Keep volunteer selection and switch to random assignment. Which claim improves, and which limitation remains?
An association needs a careful claim.

Students who choose longer study hours may also differ in preparation or motivation. A relationship between hours and scores does not isolate a causal effect. A study description must support both the intended population and the proposed cause.
Explain why observing a difference is not the same as assigning a treatment.
A college asks only volunteers in one dorm about travel to campus. Can this reliably describe all students?
The selection may miss commuters and non-volunteers.
Yes, if at least 100 people respond.
Yes, volunteering creates a randomized experiment.
Dorm volunteers may differ systematically from the full campus population. Sample size alone does not remove selection bias.
A toy population of 100 students; the survey is offered only in one dorm.
A school randomly samples students, then observes their existing sleep hours and scores. What is justified?
Population estimates may be supported, but sleep was not randomly assigned.
Random selection proves sleep causes the score difference.
Random sampling gives no useful information.
Random sampling concerns the population. This observational comparison can still be confounded.
Volunteers are randomly assigned to two teaching methods. Which claim is most careful?
A well-run trial can support a causal comparison for participants; wider generalization needs care.
This is purely observational because the participants volunteered.
The methods were assigned at random, while the participating sample remains voluntary.
Random assignment to A or B
Recruitment and treatment assignment are separate steps.
For a new study, name the population, selection method, treatment assignment, and plausible confounders.
Which group belongs in the denominator?
Separate an intersection from a conditional probability using a two-way table.

In this example one student is selected uniformly at random from the 100 listed students. Each student has the same chance. Counting favorable cases and dividing by total cases is appropriate here; equally likely outcomes cannot be assumed in every experiment.
Count all students and then count those who both joined the club and passed.
An intersection keeps the original whole.
P(club and pass) uses all 100 students as the denominator. With 12 students in the intersection, it is 12/100 = 0.12. The word “and” asks for the overlap, rather than adding the two event counts.
Keep the reference group at all students and move the overlap control.
A condition changes the reference group.

P(pass given club) considers only the 20 club members. With 12 who passed, it is 12/20 = 0.60. The numerator can stay the same while the denominator changes. Conditional probabilities in opposite directions generally differ.
Switch the reference group to club members and explain the denominator.

For events with a nonzero conditioning probability, independence means P(pass given club) = P(pass). Here 30 of 100 students passed. When 6 of the 20 club members pass, both probabilities equal 0.30. Club membership and passing are then independent in this toy table; this is not a causal claim.
Set the overlap to 6 and compare conditional and overall passing probabilities.
One of these 40 students is selected uniformly at random. What is P(pass given club)?
The condition limits the reference group to the 10 club members. Six of those 10 passed.
Rows and columns divide the same 40 students into non-overlapping cells.
One of these 50 students is selected uniformly at random. What is P(club and pass)?
Eight students satisfy both events; the reference group is all 50 students.
In this table, are passing and club membership independent?
No: events cannot overlap if they are independent.
Yes: the club caused half its members to pass.
Among club members 5/10 passed; overall 20/40 passed. The probabilities match. Independence permits overlap and does not imply causation.
Use a new two-way table to compare joint probability, both conditional directions, and independence.

Read a function as an input-output rule and preserve domain restrictions.

A function assigns exactly one output to each input in its domain. The same output may come from several inputs: x² gives 4 for both 2 and −2. That is still a function. A graph with two different y-values at one x is not a function of x.
Choose an input and describe its output, including the case where it is undefined.
For real outputs, √(x − k) needs x − k ≥ 0, so x ≥ k. The reciprocal 1/(x − k) instead needs x ≠ k. A square-root boundary may be included; a zero denominator is excluded.
Set k = 1 and compare the two rules at x = 1 and x = 0.
If f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x², f(g(2)) = f(4) = 9, while g(f(2)) = g(5) = 25. The inside rule acts first. Its output must be an allowed input to the outside rule.
Explain the difference between the two compositions using the intermediate value.

An inverse function recovers the original input. The function x² on all real inputs is not one-to-one, so it has no inverse function on that domain. Restricting x to x ≥ 0 allows the inverse √x. Keep restrictions visible when reversing or simplifying a rule.
Explain why an output of 4 does not identify a unique input for unrestricted x².
For real-valued f(x) = √(x − 2), which inputs are allowed?
The radicand must be nonnegative. x = 2 gives √0 = 0, so the boundary is included.
For f(x) = 1/(x + 3), which input is excluded?
At x = −3 the denominator is zero. All other real inputs are allowed.
Let f(x) = 3x − 1 and g(x) = x². What is f(g(2))?
First g(2) = 4, then f(4) = 12 − 1 = 11. Reversing the order would give 25.
Check domains of new radical and rational rules, then track the intermediate value in a composition.
What moves, and what changes shape?
Connect f(x − h) and vertical transformations to features of a graph.
The parent f(x) = x² has vertex (0, 0), is symmetric about x = 0, and increases away from its minimum. Matching a formula to these features is more informative than plotting a few unrelated points.
Set a = 1, h = 0, k = 0. Locate the parent vertex.
A horizontal change is inside the rule.

For y = (x − h)², the squared input becomes zero at x = h. A positive h shifts the vertex to the right. The minus sign is explained by solving x − h = 0; it is not a rule to guess from the sign alone.
Move h to 2 and explain why the vertex is at x = 2.

For y = a(x − h)² + k, k raises or lowers every output. The magnitude |a| stretches or compresses vertical distances from y = k; a negative a reflects the graph across that horizontal line. The vertex remains (h, k) when a ≠ 0.
Hold h and k fixed while switching a from 1 to −2.

Zeros occur where y = 0. For (x − 1)² − 4, the vertex is (1, −4), and zeros are x = −1 and x = 3. Between them the graph is below the axis. A graph suggests these features; substitution and algebra check the exact values.
Set h = 1 and k = −3. Predict the direction of the change before moving k again.
What is the vertex of y = (x − 2)² + 1?
The squared part is smallest at x = 2, where y = 1.
Compared with y = x², what happens in y = −2(x + 1)² + 3?
Left 1, up 3, reflected, and vertically stretched by 2.
x + 1 = x − (−1), so h = −1. The outside +3 shifts up; a = −2 reflects and stretches.
Which are the zeros of y = (x − 1)² − 9?
Set (x − 1)² = 9. Then x − 1 = ±3, so x = −2 or 4.
Describe a new transformed function using its vertex, axis, intercepts, and allowed inputs.
How does an angle become a coordinate?
Connect radians, unit-circle coordinates, and periodic sine and cosine.
A radian is arc length divided by radius. One full circle is 2π radians or 360°. Thus 180° = π radians and 90° = π/2. In calculus, derivative formulas for sine and cosine use radian inputs.
Move to 90° and read both the degree and radian measures.

On the unit circle, the point at angle θ is (cos θ, sin θ). Cosine is the horizontal coordinate; sine is the vertical coordinate. At 90°, the point is (0, 1). A positive angle turns counterclockwise from the positive x-axis.
Move to 180° and then 270°. Name the horizontal and vertical coordinates.
In quadrant II, x is negative and y is positive, so cosine is negative and sine is positive. The radius stays 1, giving cos²θ + sin²θ = 1. A negative coordinate is a direction, not a negative radius.
Move to 120°. Explain both signs from the point’s position.
A full turn repeats the coordinates.

Sine and cosine have period 2π radians. At θ and θ + 2π the unit-circle point is the same. Plotting the vertical coordinate against angle creates the sine curve. Amplitude, period, and shifts can later model repeating phenomena.
Compare 0° and 360°. Explain why they give the same sine and cosine.
At θ = 90° = π/2, what is (cos θ, sin θ)?
The point is at the top of the unit circle: horizontal coordinate 0, vertical coordinate 1.
At θ = 180° = π, which pair is correct?
The point is (−1, 0), at the left of the unit circle.
What is sin(θ + 2π) compared with sin θ?
They are equal for every real θ.
Adding one full turn returns to the same vertical coordinate. Periodicity changes the input without adding to the output.
Convert degrees to radians, predict quadrant signs, and explain a shifted or stretched periodic model.
Is the change additive or multiplicative?
Model equal-time growth with a factor and use logarithms to reverse exponentiation.
Equal differences suggest a linear rule.

The sequence 20, 30, 40 adds 10 each time. A linear rule is 20 + 10t. The sequence 20, 40, 80 multiplies by 2 each time. An exponential rule is 20 × 2ᵗ. Compare differences and ratios before choosing a model.
Compare the exponential curve with the line matched to its initial amount and first time step.
A percent change is a factor.
Growth by 50% per time unit multiplies by 1 + 0.50 = 1.5. Decay by 50% multiplies by 0.5. In y = Arᵗ, A is the amount at t = 0, and r is the factor for one time unit; it is not the amount added.
Set r = 1.5 and compare t = 0, 1, and 2.
A logarithm asks for an exponent.
logᵣ(y/A) gives the time t in y = Arᵗ, for r > 0 and r ≠ 1 and y/A > 0. For 20 × 2ᵗ = 160, we need 2ᵗ = 8, so t = log₂8 = 3. Logarithms reverse exponentiation, not multiplication.
Set A = 20 and r = 2. Find the time when the amount is 160.

Over [u, v], the average rate is [f(v) − f(u)]/(v − u), with output units per time unit. For 20 × 2ᵗ over [0, 2], it is (80 − 20)/2 = 30. A changing average rate motivates the local-rate question in Visual Calculus; it is not yet a derivative.
Compare the first-unit change with the average change over two units.
The amount is 10, 20, 40 at times 0, 1, 2. Which rule matches?
The ratios are both 2, so the amount doubles each time. The linear alternative gives 30 at t = 2.
An amount starts at 40 and decreases by 25% per hour. Which rule gives the amount after t hours?
Each hour retains 75% of the previous amount, so the factor is 0.75.
Divide by 3 to get 2ᵗ = 8. Since 2³ = 8, t = log₂8 = 3.
Choose linear or exponential models from new tables, check units, and reverse a growth rule with a logarithm.
